prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

You are reviewing layouts of one table, all rendered in a real browser with identical content, font, padding and colours; only column widths differ. You do not know who or what produced them. The first image is the content overview (every cell on one line).
Table: 2024年重点信息化项目执行情况汇总表 (language zh-CN).
Grid: 5 columns × 6 rows. Row headers: none declared.
Per-column content facts (content px at 15px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "项目" · longest unbreakable word 22px · one-line width 215px
  col 2: header "负责人" · longest unbreakable word 16px · one-line width 46px
  col 3: header "预算（万元）" · longest unbreakable word 60px · one-line width 92px
  col 4: header "进度" · longest unbreakable word 48px · one-line width 373px
  col 5: header "风险说明" · longest unbreakable word 38px · one-line width 1830px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 360px (the dashed pink box). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 359px.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

Rate EACH layout independently: "excellent" | "good" | "acceptable" | "poor" | "bad", with a short reason that points at what you see. Then name the best layout(s) (ties allowed), say how confident you are (low/medium/high), and note anything you are unsure about.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"ratings":{"A":{"grade":"","why":""},"B":{"grade":"","why":""},"C":{"grade":"","why":""},"D":{"grade":"","why":""},"E":{"grade":"","why":""},"F":{"grade":"","why":""}},"best":["letter"],"confidence":"","unsure":""}

log.raw: {"ratings":{"A":{"grade":"poor","why":"风险说明 is squeezed into a very narrow strip, making the table extremely tall; project and progress cells also fragment into short stacks that are hard to scan."},"B":{"grade":"good","why":"Best overall balance: project names and budget values remain comparatively readable, while the risk column gets enough width for continuous prose; some wrapping remains but row rhythm holds."},"C":{"grade":"acceptable","why":"Risk prose gets more room, but project, owner and budget columns are over-compressed, with names and numbers breaking awkwardly; a less balanced tradeoff."},"D":{"grade":"acceptable","why":"Project, owner and budget are reasonably legible, but the risk column is too narrow for its long text, creating tall dense rows."},"E":{"grade":"acceptable","why":"Similar to D but with an even tighter risk column; several short fields wrap awkwardly, making comparison harder."},"F":{"grade":"poor","why":"Risk gets the most space and the table is shortest, but project and owner columns collapse to one character per line, destroying the row identifiers."}},"best":["B"],"confidence":"medium","unsure":"Exact column widths are hard to measure from the scaled screenshots; B versus C is close depending on whether project identifiers or risk prose should get priority."}
